modules.title: 7.1 Rates of Reaction and Collision Theory
modules.html:
The rate of a chemical reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time:

$$\text{Rate} = \frac{\Delta[\text{product}]}{\Delta t} = -\frac{\Delta[\text{reactant}]}{\Delta t}$$

Units are usually mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. In the laboratory rate is followed by measuring the volume of gas evolved, the loss in mass, the time for a cross to disappear behind a precipitate, a change in colour (colorimetry), pH, or electrical conductivity.

Collision theory

For a reaction to occur, particles must (i) collide, (ii) collide with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy \(E_a\), and (iii) collide with the correct orientation. Only a small fraction of collisions satisfy all three conditions; these are called effective collisions.

Activation energy is the minimum energy the colliding particles must possess for the old bonds to break and new bonds to form. Reactions with a low \(E_a\) (ionic precipitations) are almost instantaneous; those with a high \(E_a\) (rusting, the reaction of \(H_2\) and \(O_2\) at room temperature) are extremely slow.

Factors affecting reaction rate

FactorEffectExplanation
Concentration (or pressure for gases)higher → fastermore particles per unit volume, so more collisions per second
Temperaturehigher → much faster (roughly doubles per 10°C)particles move faster and a much larger fraction exceed \(E_a\)
Surface areapowder reacts faster than lumpsmore particles exposed at the surface for collision
Catalystfaster (positive catalyst)provides an alternative pathway of lower activation energy
Lightspeeds photochemical reactionssupplies energy, e.g. \(H_2+Cl_2\), photosynthesis, photography
Nature of reactantsionic > covalentionic reactions need no covalent bonds broken

Catalysis

A catalyst alters the rate of a reaction but is chemically unchanged in mass and composition at the end. It lowers \(E_a\) but does not change the position of equilibrium or the enthalpy change — it merely lets equilibrium be reached sooner.

  • Homogeneous catalysis — catalyst and reactants in the same phase (\(H^+\) in ester hydrolysis).
  • Heterogeneous catalysis — different phases (Fe in the Haber process, \(V_2O_5\) in the Contact process, Ni in hydrogenation of oils).
  • Promoters increase catalyst efficiency (\(K_2O\), \(Al_2O_3\) with iron); poisons destroy it (sulphur compounds on platinum, lead on catalytic converters).
  • Enzymes are biological catalysts — extremely efficient but sensitive to temperature and pH.
  • Negative catalysts (inhibitors) slow reactions, e.g. glycerol added to hydrogen peroxide.
  • An autocatalyst is a product that catalyses its own reaction, e.g. \(Mn^{2+}\) in the \(KMnO_4\)/oxalate reaction.

examples.q: Explain, using collision theory, why powdered marble reacts faster with dilute HCl than marble chips.
examples.a: Powder has a much larger total surface area, so more CaCO₃ particles are exposed to acid particles at any instant. The frequency of effective collisions rises and the rate increases, although the total volume of CO₂ finally produced is the same.

examples.q: Why does a 10°C rise roughly double the rate of many reactions?
examples.a: Raising the temperature increases the average kinetic energy slightly, but it greatly increases the fraction of molecules whose energy exceeds the activation energy. Both the collision frequency and (mainly) the proportion of effective collisions rise.

examples.q: Does a catalyst change the yield of an equilibrium reaction? Explain.
examples.a: No. A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally by lowering \(E_a\) for both, so equilibrium is reached faster but the equilibrium position and yield are unchanged.

modules.title: 7.2 Chemical Equilibrium and Le Chatelier's Principle
modules.html:
Many reactions are reversible: products re-form reactants. When the forward and backward rates become equal, the system is at dynamic equilibrium — concentrations stay constant although both reactions continue.

Conditions for equilibrium: a closed system, constant temperature, and macroscopic properties (colour, pressure, concentration) that do not change with time.

The equilibrium constant

For \(aA + bB \rightleftharpoons cC + dD\):

$$K_c = \frac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}$$

A large \(K_c\) means the forward reaction is favoured (products predominate); a small \(K_c\) means the reactants predominate. \(K_c\) changes only with temperature — not with concentration, pressure or catalyst. For gases the equivalent constant \(K_p\) uses partial pressures. Pure solids and pure liquids are omitted from the expression.

Le Chatelier's principle

"If a constraint is imposed on a system in equilibrium, the system adjusts itself so as to annul or reduce the effect of the constraint."

ChangeShift
Increase concentration of a reactantforward, to use it up
Remove a product as it formsforward
Increase pressuretowards the side with fewer gas molecules
Increase temperaturein the endothermic direction
Add a catalystno shift
Add an inert gas at constant volumeno shift

Worked industrial applications

Haber process: \(N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3;\ \Delta H = -92\ kJ\,mol^{-1}\). High yield needs high pressure (4 molecules → 2) and low temperature (exothermic). In practice about 200 atm and 450°C with an iron catalyst are used — a compromise, because at truly low temperature the rate would be uneconomically slow.

Contact process: \(2SO_2 + O_2 \rightleftharpoons 2SO_3;\ \Delta H = -196\ kJ\,mol^{-1}\), with \(V_2O_5\) at about 450°C and 2 atm; excess air pushes the equilibrium to the right.

Bismuth chloride hydrolysis: \(BiCl_3 + H_2O \rightleftharpoons BiOCl\downarrow + 2HCl\) — adding water gives a white precipitate; adding concentrated HCl clears it again, a striking classroom demonstration.

examples.q: For \(N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2\) (\(\Delta H\) positive), predict the effect of (a) raising temperature (b) raising pressure.
examples.a: (a) The equilibrium shifts forward in the endothermic direction, so the mixture darkens as more brown NO₂ forms. (b) Higher pressure shifts it backwards towards N₂O₄, the side with fewer gas molecules, so the colour fades.

examples.q: Write the \(K_c\) expression for \(CaCO_3(s) \rightleftharpoons CaO(s) + CO_2(g)\).
examples.a: \(K_c=[CO_2]\). Pure solids do not appear in the expression because their concentrations are constant.

examples.q: At equilibrium, 2 mol \(H_2\), 2 mol \(I_2\) and 8 mol HI were present in a 1 dm³ vessel. Find \(K_c\) for \(H_2+I_2\rightleftharpoons 2HI\).
examples.a: \(K_c=[HI]^2/([H_2][I_2])=8^2/(2\times2)=64/4=16\) (no units, since the moles of gas are balanced).

modules.title: 7.3 Energy Changes: Enthalpy, Entropy and Free Energy
modules.html:
Every reaction involves breaking bonds (endothermic, absorbs energy) and making bonds (exothermic, releases energy). The net effect is the enthalpy change \(\Delta H\), measured in kJ mol⁻¹ at constant pressure.

  • Exothermic: heat is given out, \(\Delta H\) is negative, the surroundings warm up. Examples: combustion, neutralisation, respiration, rusting, dissolving NaOH or conc. \(H_2SO_4\) in water.
  • Endothermic: heat is absorbed, \(\Delta H\) is positive, the surroundings cool. Examples: photosynthesis, thermal decomposition of \(CaCO_3\), dissolving \(NH_4NO_3\) or \(KNO_3\) in water, electrolysis.

Energy profile diagrams

On an energy-level diagram the difference between reactant and product levels is \(\Delta H\); the hump between them is the activation energy \(E_a\). A catalyst lowers the hump but leaves the two levels — and therefore \(\Delta H\) — unchanged.

Standard enthalpy terms

TermDefinition
\(\Delta H_f^\ominus\) formationheat change when 1 mol of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states
\(\Delta H_c^\ominus\) combustionheat released when 1 mol of a substance burns completely in oxygen (always negative)
\(\Delta H_n^\ominus\) neutralisationheat released when 1 mol of water forms from \(H^+\) and \(OH^-\); about −57.3 kJ mol⁻¹ for strong acid + strong alkali
\(\Delta H_s^\ominus\) solutionheat change when 1 mol of solute dissolves to infinite dilution

The heat absorbed or evolved in the laboratory is calculated from

$$Q = mc\Delta\theta \qquad \Delta H = \pm\frac{Q}{n}$$

Hess's law states that the total enthalpy change for a reaction is the same whatever route is taken, provided the initial and final states are the same. It follows from the law of conservation of energy and lets us calculate values (such as \(\Delta H_f\) of methane) that cannot be measured directly.

Entropy and free energy

Entropy \(S\) measures disorder or randomness. It increases when a solid melts, a liquid vaporises, a solid dissolves, or the number of gas molecules increases; it decreases on freezing, condensing or when gas molecules combine.

Gibbs free energy decides feasibility:

$$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$$

  • \(\Delta G < 0\): the reaction is spontaneous (feasible).
  • \(\Delta G = 0\): the system is at equilibrium.
  • \(\Delta G > 0\): non-spontaneous in that direction; energy must be supplied.

Note that an exothermic reaction with a decrease in entropy may become non-spontaneous at high temperature, and an endothermic reaction with a large entropy increase (such as melting ice above 0°C) becomes spontaneous once \(T\Delta S\) exceeds \(\Delta H\).

examples.q: When 50 cm³ of 1.0 M HCl was neutralised by 50 cm³ of 1.0 M NaOH, the temperature rose by 6.8°C. Calculate \(\Delta H_n\). (c = 4.2 J g⁻¹K⁻¹, density = 1 g cm⁻³)
examples.a: Q = 100 × 4.2 × 6.8 = 2856 J = 2.856 kJ. Moles of water formed = 0.05. \(\Delta H_n = -2.856/0.05 = -57.1\ kJ\,mol^{-1}\); negative because heat was evolved.

examples.q: A reaction has \(\Delta H = +30\ kJ\,mol^{-1}\) and \(\Delta S = +150\ J\,K^{-1}mol^{-1}\). Is it feasible at 25°C?
examples.a: \(\Delta G = 30 - (298\times0.150) = 30 - 44.7 = -14.7\ kJ\,mol^{-1}\). \(\Delta G\) is negative, so the reaction is spontaneous at 298 K.

examples.q: Why is the enthalpy of neutralisation of ethanoic acid with NaOH numerically less than 57.3 kJ mol⁻¹?
examples.a: Ethanoic acid is weak; part of the heat evolved is used to complete the ionisation of the undissociated acid molecules, so less heat is available to warm the solution.

modules.title: 7.4 Oxidation–Reduction (Redox) Reactions
modules.html:
Redox has been defined in three progressively more general ways:

BasisOxidationReduction
Oxygen/hydrogengain of oxygen; loss of hydrogenloss of oxygen; gain of hydrogen
Electronsloss of electronsgain of electrons
Oxidation numberincrease in oxidation numberdecrease in oxidation number

The mnemonic OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons) — is worth memorising. Oxidation and reduction always occur together: the oxidising agent is itself reduced, and the reducing agent is itself oxidised.

Rules for assigning oxidation numbers

  1. Free elements have oxidation number 0 (\(Na\), \(O_2\), \(P_4\)).
  2. A simple ion has the oxidation number of its charge (\(Mg^{2+}=+2\), \(Cl^-=-1\)).
  3. Hydrogen is +1 except in metal hydrides (NaH) where it is −1.
  4. Oxygen is −2 except in peroxides (\(H_2O_2\), −1) and in \(OF_2\) (+2).
  5. Group 1 metals are always +1, Group 2 always +2, fluorine always −1.
  6. The sum of oxidation numbers in a neutral compound is 0; in a polyatomic ion it equals the charge.

Example: in \(KMnO_4\), \(+1 + x + 4(-2) = 0\), so Mn is +7. In \(Cr_2O_7^{2-}\), \(2x + 7(-2) = -2\), so Cr is +6.

Common oxidising and reducing agents

  • Oxidising agents: \(KMnO_4\)/H⁺ (purple → colourless), \(K_2Cr_2O_7\)/H⁺ (orange → green), \(Cl_2\), conc. \(H_2SO_4\), \(HNO_3\), \(H_2O_2\), \(O_2\), \(FeCl_3\).
  • Reducing agents: \(H_2\), C, CO, \(H_2S\), \(SO_2\), \(FeSO_4\), \(SnCl_2\), Zn, KI, \(Na_2S_2O_3\).
  • Some species are both depending on the partner: \(H_2O_2\), \(SO_2\) and \(HNO_2\).

Balancing redox equations by half-reactions

Example: \(MnO_4^-\) oxidising \(Fe^{2+}\) in acid.

$$MnO_4^- + 8H^+ + 5e^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O$$

$$Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Fe^{3+} + e^- \quad (\times 5)$$

$$MnO_4^- + 8H^+ + 5Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O + 5Fe^{3+}$$

Steps: write the two half-equations; balance atoms other than O and H; balance O with \(H_2O\); balance H with \(H^+\); balance charge with electrons; multiply so electrons cancel; add.

Disproportionation is a special case in which the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced, e.g. \(Cl_2 + 2NaOH \rightarrow NaCl + NaOCl + H_2O\) (chlorine goes from 0 to −1 and +1).

examples.q: Determine the oxidation number of sulphur in \(H_2SO_4\) and in \(Na_2S_2O_3\).
examples.a: In H₂SO₄: 2(+1)+x+4(−2)=0 ⇒ x=+6. In Na₂S₂O₃: 2(+1)+2x+3(−2)=0 ⇒ 2x=+4, so the average oxidation number of S is +2.

examples.q: In \(Zn + CuSO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + Cu\), identify the oxidising and reducing agents.
examples.a: Zn loses electrons (0 to +2): it is oxidised and is the reducing agent. Cu²⁺ gains electrons (+2 to 0): it is reduced and is the oxidising agent.

examples.q: Explain why the reaction \(Cl_2+2NaOH\rightarrow NaCl+NaOCl+H_2O\) is called disproportionation.
examples.a: Chlorine begins at oxidation number 0. In NaCl it is −1 (reduced) and in NaOCl it is +1 (oxidised). The same element is both oxidised and reduced in one reaction.

modules.title: 7.5 Electrochemistry: Electrolysis and Cells
modules.html:
Electrolytes conduct electricity in the molten or aqueous state and are decomposed by it; they contain mobile ions. Strong electrolytes (NaCl solution, dilute \(H_2SO_4\), NaOH) are fully ionised; weak electrolytes (\(CH_3COOH\), \(NH_3\) solution) only partly. Non-electrolytes (sugar solution, ethanol, benzene, kerosene) contain no ions.

Electrolysis

In an electrolytic cell, electrical energy drives a non-spontaneous reaction. The cathode is the negative electrode where cations gain electrons (reduction); the anode is positive, where anions lose electrons (oxidation).

Discharge is selective. Three factors decide which ion is discharged:

  1. Position in the electrochemical series — the ion lower in the series (less easily formed) is discharged first. Cations: \(K^+, Ca^{2+}, Na^+, Mg^{2+}, Al^{3+}, Zn^{2+}, Fe^{2+}, Pb^{2+}, H^+, Cu^{2+}, Ag^+\) (ease of discharge increases to the right). Anions: \(SO_4^{2-}, NO_3^-, Cl^-, Br^-, I^-, OH^-\).
  2. Concentration — a very concentrated chloride solution gives \(Cl_2\) rather than \(O_2\) at the anode.
  3. Nature of the electrode — inert (Pt, graphite) electrodes take no part; an active copper anode dissolves instead of releasing oxygen, which is the basis of electroplating and copper refining.

Worked examples of electrolysis

  • Molten NaCl: cathode \(Na^+ + e^- \rightarrow Na\); anode \(2Cl^- \rightarrow Cl_2 + 2e^-\) — the Downs process for sodium.
  • Concentrated brine: cathode \(2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2\); anode \(2Cl^- \rightarrow Cl_2+2e^-\); NaOH accumulates in solution — the chlor-alkali industry.
  • Dilute \(H_2SO_4\) with Pt: hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode, in the volume ratio 2:1 — effectively the electrolysis of water.
  • \(CuSO_4\) with copper electrodes: copper dissolves at the anode and plates out at the cathode; the concentration of the solution stays constant.

Faraday's laws

First law: the mass of a substance liberated at an electrode is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity passed.

$$m \propto Q, \qquad Q = It$$

Second law: when the same quantity of electricity passes through different electrolytes, the masses liberated are proportional to their chemical equivalents (molar mass / charge).

$$1\ \text{faraday} = 96500\ C = \text{charge on } 1\ \text{mole of electrons}$$

$$m = \frac{ItM}{nF}$$

Electrochemical (galvanic) cells

Here a spontaneous redox reaction produces electricity. In the Daniell cell (Zn in \(ZnSO_4\) | \(CuSO_4\) with Cu), zinc is the negative electrode (anode) and copper the positive electrode (cathode):

$$Zn + Cu^{2+} \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + Cu \qquad E^\ominus_{cell} = E^\ominus_{cathode} - E^\ominus_{anode} = 0.34 - (-0.76) = +1.10\ V$$

A positive cell e.m.f. means the reaction is feasible. Primary cells (dry Leclanché cell) cannot be recharged; secondary cells (lead–acid accumulator, lithium-ion) are rechargeable because the electrode reactions are reversible.

Applications and corrosion

Electrolysis is used for extracting reactive metals (Na, Al by the Hall–Héroult process), refining copper, electroplating, and anodising aluminium. Rusting is an electrochemical process needing both water and oxygen; it is prevented by painting, greasing, galvanising (zinc coating), and cathodic protection using sacrificial blocks of zinc or magnesium on ships and pipelines.

examples.q: Calculate the mass of copper deposited when 2 A flows for 30 minutes through \(CuSO_4\) solution. (Cu = 64)
What volume of oxygen at s.t.p. is liberated at the anode when 1 faraday passes through acidified water?
examples.a: \(4OH^-\rightarrow O_2+2H_2O+4e^-\): 4 F liberate 1 mol O₂, so 1 F gives 0.25 mol = 0.25 × 22.4 = 5.6 dm³ at s.t.p.

examples.q: Why is a zinc block bolted to the hull of a steel ship?
examples.a: Zinc is above iron in the electrochemical series, so it is oxidised in preference to the iron. It acts as a sacrificial anode, supplying electrons to the hull and protecting it from rusting; the block is replaced periodically.

quiz.solution: Rate = Δconcentration/Δtime.

quiz.solution: Solid iron catalyses a gaseous reaction — different phases.

quiz.solution: Ionic precipitations have very low activation energies.

options: the forward and reverse rates are equal
quiz.solution: Rates are equal, so concentrations remain constant.

quiz.solution: Partial pressures of the reacting gases are unchanged.

quiz.solution: Vanadium(V) oxide converts SO₂ to SO₃.

quiz.solution: The system opposes the imposed change.

quiz.solution: ΔH is negative for exothermic reactions.

quiz.solution: It absorbs light energy, so ΔH is positive.

quiz.solution: Total enthalpy change is route-independent.

quiz.solution: Mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change.

quiz.solution: A gas is far more disordered than a liquid.

quiz.q: A reaction is spontaneous when
quiz.solution: Negative Gibbs free energy indicates feasibility.

quiz.q: \(\Delta G\) is given by
quiz.solution: The Gibbs–Helmholtz relation.

quiz.q: Oxidation is best defined as
quiz.solution: OIL: oxidation is loss of electrons.

quiz.solution: Peroxides contain the O–O linkage.
